item.title: Fireworks AI's second breach in a month: what inference customers should rotate, review and ask for now
item.description: An October 24 intrusion through a cloud provider reached billing data, secrets, datasets and partial model weights, weeks after stolen internal credentials exposed customers' stored API keys.
item.content:encoded:
An October 24 intrusion through a cloud provider reached billing data, secrets, datasets and partial model weights, weeks after stolen internal credentials exposed customers' stored API keys.

Fireworks AI, the Nvidia-backed inference provider, notified customers on November 9 that an unauthorised party entered its development machines on October 24 by way of a cloud provider and reached billing data and, for some accounts, secrets, datasets and incomplete model weights, according to Bloomberg. It is the company's second disclosed security incident in little more than a month.

The two incidents

The first, which Fireworks documented in a public bulletin, began on October 6, when the company identified that someone was using internal Fireworks credentials to read environment variables from evaluation jobs in a limited number of customer accounts. Those variables included API keys and tokens customers had stored as job secrets. Fireworks rotated employee API keys on October 9, revoked affected customer keys and tokens over the following days, and emailed each identified customer a list of the credentials that needed action. Its bulletin says it found no evidence that models, datasets, training data, prompts or outputs were accessed, and notes that the platform does not store prompts or outputs by default.

The second incident, as reported, is broader: development machines rather than evaluation jobs, entry through a cloud provider rather than stolen internal credentials, and a data set that includes billing records and partial model weights. Fireworks has not published a bulletin for it as of this writing, and the number of affected customers, the cloud provider involved and whether the two intrusions are connected have not been stated.

Why inference providers are a soft target

An inference or fine-tuning platform sits on an unusual pile of value. It holds customers' credentials for other services, because evaluation and training jobs need to call out to data stores and APIs. It holds datasets uploaded for fine-tuning, and the resulting weights, which can embody months of proprietary work. And it holds billing data that reveals who is spending how much on which models. Attackers in the 'LLMjacking' economy have a direct financial motive, since stolen API keys can be resold for compute, and a stolen fine-tuned checkpoint is intellectual property that is hard to claw back.

Fireworks' own zero-data-retention default is a genuine mitigation for prompts and outputs, which is why neither incident is a privacy breach in the classic sense. The exposure is credentials and IP, and that is a different response playbook.

The counter-argument

Fireworks disclosed the first incident within days and published a detailed, dated bulletin with customer actions, which is better practice than most SaaS vendors manage. Two incidents may reflect one determined actor following a first foothold rather than systemic weakness. And customers have few alternatives: GPU-backed inference capacity is scarce enough that reports suggest customers are staying for the compute, which means switching providers in anger would cost more than hardening the relationship.

What to do

List every credential your organisation ever supplied to Fireworks as a job secret, rotate each at the issuing provider, and review that provider's access logs for the period since October 1; deleting a secret in Fireworks does nothing at the issuer. Check your Fireworks account for unrecognised API keys, users, evaluators, training jobs or datasets. If you fine-tuned models there, decide whether a partial weight leak is a reportable IP event under your policies and tell your legal team. Ask Fireworks in writing for a bulletin on the October 24 intrusion, the cloud provider involved and whether your account is in scope. Then add every model-hosting vendor to the third-party risk review you already run on your identity provider and your code host, because that is the tier of risk they now represent.

item.title: Claude Code's 'don't ask again' leaked 2,539 secrets to GitHub. A fix-it checklist
item.description: The convenience button that stops permission prompts also wrote passwords into a project file that thousands of developers committed. Here is how it happened and what to do today.
item.content:encoded:
The convenience button that stops permission prompts also wrote passwords into a project file that thousands of developers committed. Here is how it happened and what to do today.

Every coding agent asks permission before running a shell command, and every agent offers a way to stop asking. In Claude Code that option is "Yes, and don't ask again." Research published by application-security firm Apiiro and reported by The Hacker News on November 7 shows that choosing it saves the approved command, verbatim, into a file called .claude/settings.local.json inside the project. If the command contained a database URL with a password, an API token or an SSH login, that secret is now sitting in a file next to the code.

Claude Code adds the file to the user's global git excludes, but not to the project's .gitignore, so the protection does not travel with the repository. On another machine, or for a teammate, nothing stops the file being committed.

The numbers

Apiiro searched public GitHub and found 104,185 copies of the file across 103,617 repositories. About 1.1%, or 1,122 files, contained at least one secret, for 1,379 distinct secrets. More than a third opened databases directly: 379 database passwords and 122 Supabase service-role keys. There were also 43 SSH logins to public servers, some with root passwords, 42 GitHub, GitLab and npm tokens and 23 AWS keys. Sixty-three organisations were among the owners; most were individual developers.

Adding older versions of the file still in git history, the shared team-level .claude/settings.json, and saved agent transcripts, the total rose to 2,539 secrets across 1,994 repositories. Apiiro did not test whether credentials were live, but one organisation it notified confirmed its key still worked. In half the affected repositories the secret had been on the default branch for at least 217 days.

Two details should worry security teams more than the headline count. First, standard scanners did not catch most of this: Gitleaks flagged 564 of the 1,122 files and TruffleHog 643, and 215 slipped past both, because a password typed inside a shell command does not match the key formats scanners look for. Second, of 16 coding agents Apiiro compared, Claude Code was the only one confirmed to persist the full approved command in a project file by default.

Anthropic's response

Users had filed GitHub issues about this since August 2025; four were closed by an inactivity bot, the latest on November 6, without a reply. After publication, Claude Code head Boris Cherny said on Hacker News that the company is looking into it, that the tool "has not done secret scrubbing" historically, and that options include having auto mode intercept such commands or adding basic secret scanning. He also noted the file is gitignored on creation and suggested the exposed copies were committed manually. That is probably true and also beside the point: the default produced a secret-bearing file that most users did not know existed.

What to do today

Search every repository in your organisation, including history, for .claude/settings.local.json and .claude/settings.json. Treat any credential they have ever contained as compromised and rotate it before cleaning up; deleting the file does nothing for forks and clones. Untrack the file with git rm --cached and add it to the project .gitignore and to your organisation's .gitignore templates. Then change habits: reference secrets as environment variables ($DB_URL) rather than typing them into commands, and approve command patterns such as Bash(npm run:*) instead of literal commands.

For security teams, the durable fix is scope. Agent folders (.claude/, .cursor/, .gemini/) and agent memory or transcript files are secret-bearing in the same way .env is. Put them in pre-commit hooks and CI scanning with history enabled, and add rules for passwords embedded in command strings, which is the pattern that beat both open-source scanners.

What to watch

Whether Anthropic ships a scrubbing or pattern-only default, and whether other agents quietly change theirs. Apiiro's comparison of 16 agents is a useful baseline; expect follow-up research on the other 15, because the broader lesson, that agent convenience features are also data-handling features, is not specific to one vendor.

item.title: OpenAI's GPT-6 Cyber is rated 'Critical'. Here is what that means for defenders
item.description: The first model OpenAI has put in its highest cyber-capability tier is gated to vetted customers. The capability itself is not gated anywhere.
item.content:encoded:
The first model OpenAI has put in its highest cyber-capability tier is gated to vetted customers. The capability itself is not gated anywhere.

On November 5 OpenAI released GPT-6 Cyber, a version of its GPT-6 Astra flagship tuned for authorised security work: finding vulnerabilities, developing exploits to prove them, and penetration-testing web applications. The company classified it as "Critical" under its Preparedness Framework, the first time it has used the top tier for cyber capability. Its predecessor, GPT-5.6 Cyber, was rated "High".

What is actually new

Three things, according to the launch coverage:

  • Capability. OpenAI says the model outperforms GPT-6 Astra on its internal exploit benchmarks and found more than 80 previously unknown vulnerabilities in Firefox during testing. The company has not published independent evaluations.
  • Scope adherence. OpenAI says the model stayed within its authorised target scope in more than 99% of test runs. That matters because an offensive model that wanders off-scope is a liability for the customer running it, not just the target.
  • Access. The model is available only to approved customers in OpenAI's Daybreak Red programme, initially a small group, widening over the following weeks. There is no public API tier.

Why gating does not settle it

Gated release reduces casual misuse; it does not change the underlying trend. Open-weight models are a generation behind and improving, and the same month saw reports of hundreds of AI-driven hacking toolkits exposed on the open web. The practical assumption for a defender is that vulnerability discovery is becoming cheap and fast for everyone, approved or not.

That shifts the economics. Historically, the gap between a bug's existence and its discovery protected most organisations most of the time. When discovery is automated, the only gap that protects you is the one between public disclosure and your patch.

What to do this quarter

  1. Measure time-to-patch for internet-facing systems and critical dependencies. If you cannot produce the number, that is the first finding.
  2. Automate dependency updates with tests good enough to merge them without a human reading every diff.
  3. Reduce attack surface rather than racing on patches: fewer exposed services, fewer stale integrations, fewer forgotten subdomains.
  4. Use the same tools defensively. Vetted access to offensive models is available to defenders; run them against your own estate before someone else does.
  5. Brief the board in one sentence: vulnerability discovery is now automated; our defence is patch speed and surface reduction, and here is our number.

GPT-6 Cyber is one data point in a year that has produced four OpenAI security models and similar efforts from rivals. The direction is not in doubt; the question is whether your patch cadence is.
